title: Finding your service pillars and your market
audience: Any home-service operator, including solo operators, starting or growing a business.
learningOutcomes: List the skills you can sell, the topics you care about and the people who need them
Choose a core service and one or two adjacent services
Name the customer group you will serve first

instruction.heading: Start with a list, not a decision
instruction.body: Write every skill, interest and piece of experience you have. Be specific: "gutter clearing on two-storey homes" is more useful than "cleaning". Then narrow it to the skills you are paid for today or can learn quickly.

instruction.heading: Choose your pillars
instruction.body: Choose one main service and one or two supporting services that share the same customers or equipment. A pool technician who also cleans pool fences can sell both to the same households.

instruction.heading: Who needs it
instruction.body: Name the customer group, what they struggle with and what they would pay to avoid. A stronger offer comes from a narrow customer: "owners of short-stay apartments in one suburb" beats "anyone who needs cleaning".

instruction.heading: Check the market
instruction.body: Speak to five people in the customer group before you commit. Ask what they paid last time, what went wrong and what they would change.

procedure: Brainstorm skills, interests and past jobs for 20 minutes.
Mark the items that you can deliver to a paying customer now.
Pick one main service and up to two supporting services.
Name the customer group and the problem you solve for them.
Speak to five people in that group and record their answers.

workedExamples.situation: A pet sitter also grooms cats and has worked in animal rescue. Most of her clients are busy professionals who travel.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which service do you lead with?
workedExamples.reasoning: Lead with the service that the most people in the target group already pay for, and use the other skills as add-ons.

commonErrors.error: Choosing a service because it sounds profitable, not because you can deliver it well
commonErrors.prevention: Deliver a test job first and check the result with the customer.
Name one customer group for the first six months.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business guidance only. This lesson does not grant any licence, registration or authority. Check state or territory rules before acting.

qualityStandard: Offer and pricing decisions are written down and checked against cost and time.
documentationEvidence: Written offer or plan, evidence collected, and the decision made.
summary: Lead with one main service and a clearly named customer group.
Test the market by speaking to real customers before committing.

knowledgeChecks.question: What makes a good first customer group?
options: Everyone who owns a house in the city
A narrow group with a clear, paid problem
Anyone who replies to an advert today

knowledgeChecks.question: Why choose one main service?
options: It avoids all competition in the area
It removes the need for pricing at all
It makes the offer and the marketing clearer
It means no testing is needed at all today

knowledgeChecks.question: What should you do before committing to a service?
options: Buy new equipment before you speak
Sign a shop lease before you speak
Publish a website with no testing
Speak to five people in the target group

sourceReferences: Solopreneur Start-Up Guide, Step 2 (Tom Scourfield; distribution rights held by the user). Adapted for home-service operators; sales pitch at the end of the guide omitted.
